rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

examples: This non-opening story card has three sentences: the ground waiting, God not using gold or marble, and the teaser about the humbler material. Trim it to one or two sentences.
This story card has three sentences, including Papa Dorin's comment about the 25 cent bin. Condense it to one or two sentences.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: “ANY tree?”, the parking comparison, and the woman's correction. Non-opening story cards are limited to one or two sentences.

places.problem: This non-opening story card has three sentences: the ground waiting, God not using gold or marble, and the teaser about the humbler material. Trim it to one or two sentences.
This story card has three sentences, including Papa Dorin's comment about the 25 cent bin. Condense it to one or two sentences.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: “ANY tree?”, the parking comparison, and the woman's correction. Non-opening story cards are limited to one or two sentences.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: Cain's statement, “Heavy words, friend.” and “Let them sit a second.”
This story card has four sentences. Summarizing the genealogy and trades in one card is appropriate, but the summary is still over the story-card sentence limit.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: one about Shem, one about Peleg and Joktan, and one about Papa Dorin's cutters.

This non-opening story card has three sentences: the scattering statement, 'Big plans, baker,' and 'Bigger God.' The closing quip needs to be combined into one sentence or otherwise shortened to keep the card within the two-sentence limit.
This genealogy summary is three sentences long. Since it is not the stop's opening card, it exceeds the two-sentence limit for story cards.
This non-opening story card is punctuated as three sentences: the preparation sentence, "Early, friend." and "The very next morning."
This story card is punctuated as three sentences: the settlement sentence, "Me?" and the mustache punchline.
The genealogy summary, the Rebekah detail and the story-continuation line make three sentences on a non-opening story card.
This non-opening story card has three sentences, exceeding the one-to-two-sentence limit.
This story card has four sentences, exceeding the one-to-two-sentence limit.
This story card has three sentences, exceeding the one-to-two-sentence limit.

This non-opening story card has three sentences: "And once more, son number four: Judah.", "FOUR, friend.", and "At this rate Leah's gonna need a bigger tent." Story cards after the opening card are limited to one or two sentences.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the statement about the three-day journey, the burnt-cookie question, and the zip-code punchline. It needs to be shortened to one or two sentences.

This non-opening story card has three sentences: the narrative sentence, 'A family meeting in a field full of sheep.' and 'Friend, that is a LOT of listeners.' It needs to be reduced to one or two sentences.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the angel's quoted statement, 'In other words: Jacob, you KNOW Me.' and 'We've met.' It needs to be reduced to one or two sentences.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the pursuit and arrival, "Seven days, friend!", and the joke about Papa Dorin's base. That exceeds the two-sentence limit.

This non-opening story card exceeds the sentence limit. "Four hundred men.", "FOUR.", and "HUNDRED." already create three sentence-like units before the final sentence about Jacob dividing the children.
This non-opening story card has four sentences, exceeding the two-sentence limit.
This non-opening story card has four sentences, exceeding the two-sentence limit.
This non-opening story card has three sentences, exceeding the two-sentence limit.
This non-opening story card has three sentence units: Joseph's reply, "Me?", and the alarm-and-snooze sentence.
This non-opening story card has three sentence units: the robe-stripping sentence, "THE robe.", and "The robe of many colors he's wearing."
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the attribution accompanying "No," the Sheol quotation, and the sentence about Jacob weeping and Papa Dorin missing his kids.
This non-opening story card has three sentences or sentence fragments: the main sentence, "Well." and "Almost any of it." That exceeds the two-sentence limit.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the question “And the chief baker?”, the sentence about his being hanged, and the concluding sentence about both interpretations coming true.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the sentence about collecting and storing the grain, the question ending in “and me?”, and the sentence about payday and the couch cushions.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the sentence about the famine, the question about the man selling grain, and the sentence identifying Joseph.
This story card has three sentences: the opening question, the sentence about the missing brother, and the group-chat joke.

This story card exceeds the limit with three sentences of narration: the introduction to Jacob's quotation, "Friend, I know that feeling," and the sentence about the junk drawer. Jacob's quotation also contains two sentences.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: Israel gives in, he instructs his sons about the gift, and Papa Dorin adds a joke. It needs to be condensed to one or two sentences.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the vision, the dough joke, and Jacob's answer. Non-opening story cards are limited to one or two sentences.
This summary has three sentences: the description of the list, "Seventy in all.", and the cookie-cutter joke. That exceeds the two-sentence limit for a non-opening story card.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the exclamation about Jacob's age, the junk-drawer reaction, and the setup for his burial request.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the embalming statement, the one-word sentence FORTY., and the oven joke.
This story card has three sentences: Joseph's return, Promise kept, friend., and the final CAME BACK sentence.

This story card has three sentences: “Pharaoh wants Moses dead.”, “So Moses does what anybody would do, friend.”, and “He RUNS.” Only the opening card may have up to three sentences; this card needs to be reduced to one or two sentences.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the travel sentence, the question about the donkey, and the junk-drawer reaction.
This is not the walkthrough's opening card, but it has three sentences: the LORD's instruction, “That's the WHOLE address,” and the sentence about having no pin or landmark.
The card runs beyond the two-sentence limit with the gathering sentence, the meeting question, “Yeah.” and “THAT moment.”
This story card has three sentences: “SLACKERS!”, “Slackers!”, and the sentence beginning “And that's why”. Since this is not an opening card, it exceeds the two-sentence limit.

This non-opening story card exceeds the two-sentence limit. Even treating "FROGS. IN. THE. OVENS." as one emphatic outburst rather than four fragments, it is followed by two additional full sentences.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: "And not just a few.", the statement about all the dust turning into gnats, and the junk-drawer joke. Combine or trim them to two.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the question about asking for silver and gold, the coupon joke, and the teaser about the Egyptians' reaction.
This non-opening story card has three full sentences plus a question fragment, exceeding the limit of one or two sentences.

This non-opening story card has four sentences: the summary, the donkey and eye-for-eye details, the cookie-dough sentence, and 'I looked.' Condense it to no more than two sentences while retaining the long-stretch summary.
This non-opening story card has four sentences, exceeding the one-to-two-sentence limit.
This story card has three sentences: “Altar's up.” “Pillars are up.” and the sentence about the offerings. It exceeds the one-to-two-sentence limit.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the goat-hair tent sentence, "That's my kind of instructions, friend," and the recipe sentence.
This story card has three sentences: "It's a land flowing with milk and honey," "Sounds perfect, right?" and "Then God says the next part...." Only the opening card may have three sentences.
This story card is punctuated as three sentences: the Israelites stripping off their jewelry, "Me?" and the sentence about flour in Papa Dorin's mustache. It exceeds the two-sentence limit.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the rule about the flesh and clay pot, the standalone exclamation "BROKEN!", and the junk-drawer joke.
This story card has three sentences: the third-day warning, the question ending in "but this meat?", and "Hands OFF."
This non-opening story card has three standalone sentences or utterances: 'Moses hears Aaron out...', 'Me?', and 'Somebody explains themselves...'. That exceeds the two-sentence limit.
This non-opening story card runs to four sentences: the statement about touching things, the question about carrying them, the command to wash and bathe, and the moving-crew punchline.

This non-opening story card runs to four short sentences or sentence fragments: the Scripture statement, "Complete rest.", "No oven, no timer, NOTHING." and the mustache line. It needs to be condensed to one or two sentences.

This non-opening story card has three sentences: "Then comes a long list," the summary of the prohibitions, and the sentence about the reasons God gives. It needs to be condensed to no more than two sentences.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the statement about revenge and grudges, the question about the replacement stamper, and the quoted reply.
This non-opening story card runs beyond two sentences: the quotation itself contains two sentences, followed by the separate lines “No fine print, friend.” and “No 'terms may vary.'”
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the statement about God calling the Israelites His servants twice, the sentence about Egypt and His closing words, and the continuation line.
This non-opening story card has three sentences or sentence fragments: the diseases and fever, "And those harvests that ran into each other?" and "Now they'll sow their seed in vain."
This non-opening story card has four sentences or sentence fragments: the opening statement about the bread, "TEN bakers.", "ONE oven.", and "Friend, let that sink in."
This story card has five sentences. Only the opening card may be longer than two sentences.
This story card has four sentences. Only the opening card may be longer than two sentences.
This non-opening story card runs three sentences: the narration followed by "A whole TRIBE, friend." and "Presented to ONE man."
This story card runs four sentences, including the two-sentence jealousy joke, exceeding the two-sentence limit.
This story card runs three sentences: Moses' obedience, the reaction to the one-month age threshold, and the roster joke.
The long-stretch summary runs five sentences. Being a summary makes the stretch one beat, but it does not exempt the card from the one-to-two-sentence limit.
This story card runs four sentences, including the two short number statements and the two-sentence cookie-box joke.

This non-opening story card has three sentences: the sentence about counting the Gershonites, "The LORD is consistent, and me?" and the sentence about Papa Dorin's cookie batches. Non-opening story cards are limited to one or two sentences.
Non-opening story cards 3, 5, 6, 8, 12 and 15 each exceed two sentences. Card 3 runs to five short punctuated sentences and card 6 to four; the others run to three.
Story cards 1, 5 and 9 each exceed the two-sentence limit for non-opening story cards.

This non-opening story card has three sentences: the introduction to line three, the standalone exclamation "Peace!", and the sentence about the batteries. Non-opening story cards are limited to one or two sentences.
This non-opening story card has three sentences, exceeding the two-sentence limit.

This non-opening story card has at least three sentences: the quarrel, "Friend, I know that voice," and the flat-batch joke. That exceeds the one-to-two-sentence limit even before counting the additional sentence inside Papa Dorin's quoted joke.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: Moses' intercession, "That's a big heart, friend," and the group-chat joke. Non-opening story cards are limited to one or two sentences.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the poets' quotation, the sentence about the drawer, and "Sihon's city gets a whole one."
Several non-opening story cards exceed two sentences: stop 1 cards 6 and 15, and stop 2 cards 1, 9, 11 and 13.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: “And not just any strength.” “Strength like a wild ox.” “Then Balaam turns to the subject of spells and divination.”
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the order to count, the pencil line, and "A BIG one." That exceeds the two-sentence limit.
This non-opening story card runs to four sentence-length units: "Count's done.", the inheritance sentence, "See?", and "The counting PAYS OFF." It needs to be compressed to one or two sentences.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the LORD answering, the comment about God weighing in, and "Ohhh, baker, it is getting GOOD."
Several non-opening story cards exceed the two-sentence limit: stop 1 card 7 and stop 2 cards 1 and 2 each have three sentences, while stop 2 card 8 has four.
Several non-opening story cards run to three sentences when their short reaction lines are counted: stop 1 cards 3, 8 and 12; stop 2 card 9; and stop 3 cards 6, 11 and 15.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the statement about crossing the Jordan, the question about paying guests and the line addressed to Sihon. That exceeds the two-sentence limit.

This non-opening story card has four punctuated sentence units: the statement about God giving the cities, the statement about the walls, "Me?" and the takeout-menu sentence. That exceeds the two-sentence limit.
This non-opening story card has five sentences, exceeding the one-to-two-sentence limit.
This story card has four sentences, exceeding the one-to-two-sentence limit.
This story card has four sentences, exceeding the one-to-two-sentence limit.
This story card has six sentences. It is not the walkthrough's opening card, so it exceeds the one-to-two-sentence limit.
This story card has three sentences, exceeding the one-to-two-sentence limit.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the statement about Egypt, 'Iron furnace, friend.' and the oven punchline. It needs to be tightened to one or two sentences.

This non-opening story card has three sentences: the statement about the man-made gods, the question about smelling a fresh batch and the cookie-stamper punchline. It needs to be tightened to one or two sentences.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the list of locations, "Every green tree, friend!", and the dust-drawer joke. That exceeds the two-sentence limit.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the sacrifice's source, Moses being particular about the location, and "Not 'eh, wherever.'" That exceeds the two-sentence limit.
This story card has three sentences: the arrival of the Feast of Weeks, the seven weeks of counting, and the junk-drawer joke. That exceeds the two-sentence limit.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: Moses and the priests speaking, the nation-sized crowd, and the mixer joke.
This story card has three period-ended sentences: the curse, the restatement about taking money, and Papa Dorin's reaction.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: 'Nope.', the statement about lending and borrowing, and the payment-email joke. Story cards other than the opening card are limited to two sentences.

This non-opening story card exceeds two sentences: the opening statement about the stars, the sentence about losing count of the sprinkles, and then 'The stars?' and 'Forget it.' The joke can remain while being compressed into the two-sentence limit.
This non-opening story card has three sentence units: the crowd description, the setup ending with "and honestly?" and "He left EARLY." Non-opening story cards are limited to one or two sentences.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: 'And not halfway, either.', 'With all their heart and all their soul, Moses says.', and 'Then it's God's move.' That exceeds the two-sentence limit.
This story card has four sentence units, including 'Not them.' and 'The LORD.', rather than the permitted one or two sentences.
This story card has three sentence units: the opening question, 'They don't just vanish.', and 'They get a NEW ADDRESS.' It needs to fit within two sentences.
This story card has four sentences: the statement about the land, the oven-timer setup, and separate sentences about listening and ignoring the timer. That exceeds the two-sentence limit.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: one about proclaiming the LORD's name, one about the solid name, and one beginning "Doesn't move, doesn't crack."
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the retelling of verse 7, "Friend, nobody has to ask ME twice.", and the sentence about junk drawer stories.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the sentence about wandering, "Forty YEARS.", and the junk-drawer joke.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the LORD's statement, the PAST DUE question, and "Like THAT, times a thousand."
This non-opening story card is five sentences long: the quoted sentence followed by four more sentences. It exceeds the two-sentence limit.

This non-opening story card has three sentences: the verse 27 update, the apron instruction, and the sentence saying that more of the story is coming. It needs to be compressed to two sentences while retaining the required continuation line.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the introduction of Sihon and Og, the price-sticker joke, and the statement about Moses and the Israelites striking them down.
This non-opening summary story card has three sentences: the description of the western land, the roll call of kings, and the joke about the total.
This non-opening story card runs to four sentences, including "Yes, friend." and "THAT Jerusalem."
The closing story card has four sentences rather than the permitted one or two.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: "But hold on.", "Hold on, hold on, HOLD ON.", and the following "What if..." question. Non-opening story cards are limited to one or two sentences.
This long-stretch summary runs for four dense sentences, although a non-opening story card is limited to 1 to 2 sentences. It needs to be condensed while remaining one summary card for the stretch.
This story card has four sentences: the two 'Hold on' sentences, the sentence about Israel's trouble, and the sentence about the LORD raising up judges.
The opening sentence, the statement about the LORD raising a judge with 'EVERY. SINGLE. TIME.' broken into separate pieces, and the closing rescue sentence run past the two-sentence limit.
'Now it gets quiet, friend.' and 'Real quiet.' are followed by the longer sentence about the LORD's anger and speech, making three sentences.
'Ohhh.' plus the two sentences that follow gives this story card three sentences.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the numbers leaving and remaining, "I've seen that move, friend," and the boss-and-parking-lot sentence.
Story cards 1, 7 and 9 each contain three sentences. None is the walkthrough's opening card, so each is limited to one or two sentences.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the fact about Gideon's sons, Papa Dorin's joke, and the setup about Abimelech's question.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: "Big talk.", the group-chat comparison, and the sentence about Zebul hearing Gaal and burning with anger.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: "Round one is over.", the sentence about Abimelech and Zebul, and the joke about Gaal not unpacking.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: "Jephthah's in charge now.", "His first move?", and "He sends messengers to the king of the Ammonites."
This story card has three sentences: the account of Israel's detour, "A WHOLE nation on a detour.", and the GPS punchline. It is not the opening card, so it is limited to two sentences.

The final story card has three sentences: the summary of the king's response, "Keep that oven warm, baker.", and "We are NOT done with Jephthah yet." The story-isn't-over line does not create an exception to the two-sentence limit.
This non-opening story card has three sentences. Trim or combine the storyteller line and joke so the card stays within two sentences.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the capture of the fords, the line about crossing the river, and the airport-security joke.
This non-opening story card runs to four sentences, including "SEVENTY." The summary and its joke need to fit within two sentences.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the angel's arrival, "Not to Manoah." and "To his wife." That exceeds the two-sentence limit.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the razor statement, "No razor, friend." and the mustache reaction. It needs to be compressed to one or two sentences.
This story card has three sentences. Only the walkthrough's opening card may be that long; this is the opening of the second stop, not the opening card of the walkthrough.

This story card is written as four standalone sentences or sentence fragments: the bowstrings, the ropes, the scam-call comparison, and Delilah's renewed question. That exceeds the two-sentence limit.
The emphatic 'Every day. EVERY. DAY.' followed by the closing sentence gives this story card four standalone sentences or fragments, exceeding the two-sentence limit.

This non-opening story card exceeds two sentences: after the sentences about returning the silver and the curse and blessing, it adds a separate question fragment and the standalone punchline 'SAME GUY.'

This non-opening story card has three sentences: "They stay there four months.", "Four MONTHS on a rock.", and the sentence about Papa Dorin's years in the junk drawer. That exceeds the two-sentence limit.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: Boaz's greeting, the workplace joke, and the harvesters' reply.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the fork action, "This man is NOT picky, friend," and "If it's boiling, he's in it." That exceeds the two-sentence limit.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: "Five more children," "FIVE," and the sentence about Samuel growing up. It needs to fit within two sentences.
This non-opening story card exceeds the two-sentence limit: "The GROUND." and "SHAKES." are separate sentence units, followed by the sentence about Mags and the Philistines.
This non-opening story card has three sentences, exceeding the two-sentence limit.
This non-opening story card has three sentences, exceeding the two-sentence limit.
This non-opening story card has four sentences: the two quoted sentences and the two snooze-button sentences. It exceeds the two-sentence limit.
Even without counting the fragment 'But WHO?', this non-opening story card has four sentences. The story-continuation line does not exempt it from the two-sentence limit.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: Samuel's "Stop!", his statement about telling Saul what the LORD said, and Saul's reply.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: Samuel's question, the rhetorical question about replacing Saul, and the workplace comparison. It exceeds the two-sentence limit.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the peace reply, the statement about coming to sacrifice, and the instruction to consecrate themselves. It exceeds the two-sentence limit.
This story card has three sentences: Jesse's report about his youngest son, the question about being stuck out back, and Papa Dorin's drawer reaction. It exceeds the two-sentence limit.
This story card has three sentences: the youngest son's arrival and description, the interjection calling for a pause, and the callback about Eliab. It exceeds the two-sentence limit.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: Saul's command, "And one of the servants?" and "He already knows a guy."
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the message to Jesse, the comment about David being out in a field, and the CEO comparison.

This non-opening story card has three sentences: the move to Bethlehem, Jesse's family, and the three oldest brothers following Saul. Story cards after the opening are limited to one or two sentences.
This non-opening story card is broken into three sentences: the stone sinking and Goliath falling, "Six cubits and a span, flat on his face.", and "ONE stone." It exceeds the two-sentence limit.
This non-opening story card has four sentence-length units: the opening statement, "Saul.", "LISTENS.", and Papa Dorin's closing reaction. That exceeds the two-sentence limit.
This non-opening story card has three sentences once Saul's two-sentence quotation is included: the idol setup, Saul's question, and his accusation.
This non-opening story card has three sentence-length units: its opening summary, the question fragment about Saul and David, and "It's nowhere near done."
This non-opening story card has three sentences: Jonathan's answer, the assurance that he would tell David, and David's follow-up question.
The seating sentence, "And David's seat?" and "EMPTY, and nothing at a dinner table talks louder than an empty chair" make three sentence units on a non-opening story card.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the report about David's followers, "Friend, that's not an army," and the DMV punchline.
This non-opening story card exceeds two sentences. Gad's quotation contains two sentences, followed by a separate sentence about David leaving and another sentence for the snooze-button joke.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: Saul's complaint, "Not ONE," and the group-chat joke.
This story card exceeds two sentences: the résumé sentence is followed by Ahimelech's quoted question and the separate exclamation, "Far be it from me!"
This final story card has three sentences: the two sentences quoted from David and the additional story-continuation sentence.

This non-opening story card has three sentences: the sentence about Achish trusting David, the sentence about the Philistines gathering for war, and the standalone "Uh-oh." Non-opening story cards are limited to one or two sentences.
Several non-opening story cards exceed two sentences: stop 1 cards 7 and 9 each have four, stop 1 card 11 has three when Saul's two quoted sentences are counted, and stop 2 card 19 has three.
This non-opening story card has three sentences.

This non-opening story card has three sentences: "They journey all night to get them.", "All night, friend.", and "I can't make it past the second oven timer without nodding off." That exceeds the two-sentence limit.

This non-opening story card has three sentences: the narration about the messengers, "No text, no group chat, friend.", and the final joke. Non-opening story cards are limited to one or two sentences.
This non-opening story card runs well past two sentences. Joab's quotation contains several sentences, and Papa Dorin adds two more sentences after it.
This is not the passage's opening card, but it uses three sentences: one about Abner's death, one about David's orders, and one joke about Joab's assignment.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the Jebusites' thought, the chocolate-chip-bin comparison, and "Famous last words." It exceeds the two-sentence limit.

This story card runs for more than two sentences, including the separate exclamation "ELEVEN!" and the closing bakery joke. The long-stretch summary rule does not exempt it from the story-card sentence limit.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the Hadadezer sentence, the cooling-rack setup, and “The cooling rack won.”
This non-opening story card has three sentences: Joab's quotation, "Fight hard, then leave it with the LORD," and "That's the whole plan."

This non-opening story card has three sentences: Ziba's response, the comment about the donkeys and Mephibosheth's property, and the workplace comparison. Non-opening story cards are limited to two sentences.
This non-opening story card has four sentences, exceeding the two-sentence limit.
This is not an opening card, but it has three sentences: the introduction to the list, the sentence about Uriah, and "Thirty-seven in all."
Several non-opening story cards exceed the sentence limit: card 4 has four sentences, card 9 has three, card 10 has four, and card 12 has three.
This non-opening story card has three sentences when "Me?" is counted, exceeding the two-sentence limit.
This story card is punctuated as five sentences, including "Me?" and "Twenty-five cents.", well beyond the two-sentence limit for a non-opening story card.
This non-opening story card runs for six sentences, including the Gezer explanation and the two-sentence wedding-gift joke. It needs to be condensed to the bite-sized limit.

This story card has four sentences, counting the closing joke. It also stacks the yearly revenue, shields, cups, ship cargo, throne and lions in one dense card rather than keeping the summary to the two-sentence limit.
This story card has four sentences: the tribute, the chariots and silver, the import and export trade, and the parking joke. That exceeds the limit for a non-opening story card.

This non-opening story card has three sentences: the sentence listing the women and nations, followed by two separate joke sentences. It needs to be trimmed or combined into no more than two sentences.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: two inside Ahijah's quoted greeting and then Papa Dorin's joke about the disguise.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: "Then Elijah picks up stones." "Twelve of them, friend." "Not eleven, not thirteen." That exceeds the two-sentence limit.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the instruction from Jezebel's letter, the question about the seat of honor, and "I don't trust it."
This non-opening story card has three sentences: "Naboth is gone.", the report sent to Jezebel, and "And Jezebel goes to her husband."
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the introduction of Jehoshaphat and the king of Israel, "Two kingdoms, side by side." and "So how do these two get along?"
This non-opening story card has three sentences: "Wrecked at Ezion-geber.", "Never even left." and the sentence carrying Papa Dorin's dough-tray comparison.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the recap of the death message, the line about Ahaziah's next question, and the question about the man's appearance.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: Ahaziah not needing another clue, his identification of Elijah, and the business-card joke.
This non-opening story card runs to three sentences or sentence fragments: the narrative setup, 'Fifty men.', and 'For one hairy guy who is SITTING DOWN.'

This non-opening story card has three sentences: Elisha's initial reply, "Do not speak of it," and the separate sentence introducing Elijah's next request. Non-opening story cards are limited to two sentences.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the narration about the prophets at Jericho, the oven-timer comparison ending in "I KNOW," and the final standalone "I KNOW."
This non-opening story card has three sentences: Jehoshaphat's pledge, 'THAT is a friend,' and the question about which route to take. The limit is two sentences.

The retrieval, the drawer comparison and the extended jealousy punchline run well beyond two sentences. Even without counting the emphatic "IRON. FLOATING." fragments, the card exceeds the story-card sentence limit.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the reaction "Yep.", the statement that Jeroboam does evil, and the sentence about restoring Israel's borders.
This story card has three sentences: "Back up north.", the sentence introducing Zechariah's reign, and "Friend, don't get too attached to this one." It is not the walkthrough's opening card.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: "Six months.", the sentence about Zechariah's evil, and the sentence introducing Shallum's conspiracy.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the summary of the list, 'And the Sepharvites go further,' and the sentence about their child sacrifice. It needs to be no more than two sentences.
This non-opening story card has three sentences: the quoted verse, "One night." and "That's all it took, friend."
This story card has three sentence units: "That's the message.", "Straight, no sprinkles.", and "So Hezekiah turns his face to the wall." A non-opening story card is limited to one or two sentences.
This non-opening story card uses three separate sentences or sentence fragments: "The king stops." "Looks." "And asks, 'What is this monument I see?'"
Five non-opening story cards exceed the two-sentence limit: card 4 has five sentences, card 5 has three, card 8 has three, card 10 has four and card 12 has five.
This non-opening story card runs for four sentences, including the Elkanah joke and the detail about Samuel's sons. It exceeds the one-to-two-sentence limit.
This story card introduces all three singers, summarizes their positions and then tells a multi-sentence oven joke. It runs well beyond the two sentences allowed for a non-opening story card.

rule.text: The rule against guessing the next words of a line (see below) applies to every passage, and to fill in the blank too. The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.

examples: The earlier cards have said only that their eyes were opened. They have not mentioned nakedness or a need for coverings, so the baker cannot reason out “naked”; the blank tests unseen wording.

The setup quotes the general curse but gives no context from which the serpent's new movement can be inferred. “Belly” is therefore an unseen word the baker must guess rather than a meaning supported by the earlier cards.
Card 1 says only that Adam gives his wife a name. Nothing in the earlier cards allows the baker to reason out “Eve,” so this blank simply asks for an unseen name.

places.problem: The earlier cards have said only that their eyes were opened. They have not mentioned nakedness or a need for coverings, so the baker cannot reason out “naked”; the blank tests unseen wording.

The setup quotes the general curse but gives no context from which the serpent's new movement can be inferred. “Belly” is therefore an unseen word the baker must guess rather than a meaning supported by the earlier cards.
Card 1 says only that Adam gives his wife a name. Nothing in the earlier cards allows the baker to reason out “Eve,” so this blank simply asks for an unseen name.

The earlier cards give no basis for reasoning out 120 rather than 365 or 969. This blank asks the baker to supply an unseen number, so the answer depends on luck rather than an understanding they can reason out.

The unexplained mention of the Nephilim gives the baker no basis for choosing mighty over faithful or humble. The blank therefore asks for unseen wording instead of a meaning the baker can reason out from the earlier cards.

The blank asks for an unrevealed detail. The preceding story card mentions only Abram's former tent site, so a baker using only the earlier cards has no basis for reasoning out “altar” rather than “well” or “tower.” This is a guess at wording not yet seen.

The earlier cards say only that Lot settled in the cities of the plain. They provide no clue from which a baker could reason out “Sodom” rather than “Jericho” or “Bethel,” so this blank asks for an unseen place name rather than a meaning the baker can infer.

The blank asks the baker to supply the unseen BSB word "blessed" and complete the wording of verse 18. The earlier cards do not establish what will come to the nations through Abraham, so this is a next-words guess rather than a blank whose meaning can be reasoned out.

The setup says only that Abraham is choosing the baby's name. Nothing in the earlier cards supplies Isaac's name or a clue from which to infer it, so Jacob and Joseph are just as plausible to a baker who does not already know the passage.
The earlier cards establish only that Abraham is old. Sixty, eighty and a hundred all fit that description, and no setup gives the baker a reasoned way to choose his exact age.

The preceding cards establish mocking and Sarah's demand for expulsion, but they say nothing about inheritance or otherwise set up that concern. The baker is asked to supply an unseen word rather than reason out a meaning from the setup.

No earlier card positively tells the baker what God intends to make of Ishmael. Card 8 merely rules out the statement that nothing will come of him, leaving no basis for reasoning that nation, rather than army or city, completes this promise.
Nothing in the earlier cards points toward archery. Growing up in the wilderness does not make archer clearly more inferable than shepherd, so the baker must guess the unseen wording of verse 20.
The blank asks for the unseen wording “full price.” Nothing in cards 1-7 establishes whether Abraham wants to pay full, half or a low price, so the baker cannot reason out the blank from its meaning.
With no clue about the metal in the earlier cards, the baker can only guess the next word of Ephron's statement. “Shekels” does not give the baker a basis for choosing silver over gold or bronze.

The blank asks for the unrevealed place name in "Mount ___." Nothing in the setup lets the baker reason out Zion, so this tests wording the baker has not seen rather than meaning they can infer.

Card 4 says only that Asaph gives God a reason, providing no basis for choosing "name" over "temple" or "city." The blank therefore tests wording the baker has not seen rather than a meaning they can reason out.

Neither card 8 nor any earlier card introduces enemies or a promise of victory. The baker therefore cannot reason out "foes"; the blank simply asks for wording from verse 14 that has not yet been shown.

The blank simply asks for the unseen wording of verse 3. The earlier cards establish only that God's enemies rage; they do not establish that the target is God's people, so the baker cannot reason out "people" rather than "temple" or "prophets."

The earlier cards give no context from which to reason out "oil." The blank simply asks for unseen wording from verse 20, resembling the walkthrough's example of the unsuitable question about what David was anointed with.

Neither the earlier cards nor the setup 'God sends help' gives the baker a way to reason out 'angels' rather than 'prophets' or 'priests'. The blank tests unseen wording by luck instead of a meaning established by the setup.

This completes the BSB line's wording by asking for its unread final word, “strength.” The earlier cards establish the LORD's reign and majesty, but they do not set up enough for the baker to reason out this detail rather than guess the wording.
The card asks the baker to complete the psalm's exact wording, “from all ___,” with the unread word “eternity,” making it a next-word completion of the line.
The card reproduces the end of the BSB line and asks for its unread final word, “majestic,” making the baker complete the line's wording.

The blank asks for the exact BSB word "proclaimed," which has not appeared in any earlier card. Although the alternatives make one choice more plausible, the card is still testing wording the baker has not seen rather than a meaning established by the setup.

Several blanks test wording that cannot be inferred from the earlier cards: Isaac in stop 1 card 12, Canaan in stop 1 card 14, Egypt in stop 2 card 11, blood in stop 3 card 5 and rock in stop 3 card 16. The setup needed to reason out each answer has not yet been given.

The earlier cards describe Israel's sin at Baal of Peor but give no basis for choosing a plague rather than a famine or a battle. This blank therefore tests the unseen wording of verse 29 instead of a meaning the baker can reason out.

The two blanks ask the baker to complete the unseen wording of David's last line with "valor" and "trample." The preceding cards do not establish those specific ideas well enough to reason them out, so this becomes guessing the line's wording rather than testing its movement or meaning.

The baker is asked to complete the unseen wording of verse 5, "full of ___." Compassion, power and wisdom are all plausible things to say about God after a rescue, so this becomes a guess at the line's final word rather than a question about its movement or meaning.

The card simply asks the baker to supply the unseen last word of the psalmist's line to his soul by completing "return to its ___." That is wording completion rather than a meaningful question about why he speaks to his soul or what has changed.

The question asks the baker to complete the unseen ending of verse 16, "He has broken his ___." The setup about calling himself the LORD's servant does not turn this into a question about the verse's movement or meaning; it remains a guess at the line's final word.

The blank asks for the unseen BSB wording “free.” The preceding story card says only that the writer called to the LORD in distress, and all three options can complete “set him,” so this is a wording guess rather than a blank grounded enough in the passage's meaning.

This asks for the unseen next word of the line rather than a meaning the baker can reason out. Card 1 says that the psalmist cried to the LORD, but it gives no basis for choosing how the LORD responded.

This fill-in-the-blank asks the baker to supply the exact wording of an unseen line from the psalm. The preceding story card only says that some people take a turn, so completing "crooked" tests recall of wording rather than meaning the baker can reason out.

This blank asks for wording the baker has not seen. The restoration and dreamlike reaction in cards 1-2 do not establish why the singers' mouths were filled with laughter rather than silence or sighing, so this is a wording guess rather than a question about the psalm's movement or meaning.
Nothing in the preceding cards lets the baker reason out that the saying was among the nations rather than the priests or elders. The blank simply supplies an unseen detail from the verse.

This asks the baker to supply the unseen word "table" from the psalm's next line. The preceding setup introduces the wife-and-vine picture but says nothing about the sons, so this blank tests an unheard detail of the wording rather than a meaning the baker has been equipped to reason out.

The opening card says only that the songwriter asks the LORD to remember something for David. It gives no context from which to reason out “hardships” rather than “journeys” or “years,” so the blank tests unseen wording.

The preceding card discusses only the priests being clothed with righteousness. It provides no basis for inferring that the saints shout for “joy” rather than “help” or “mercy,” making this a guess at the psalm's unseen wording.

The setup deliberately withholds the place name, and no earlier card allows the baker to reason out “Zion” rather than “Shiloh” or “Bethel.” The blank therefore tests an unseen place name rather than an inferable meaning.

The earlier cards do not give the baker a way to infer "wonderful" rather than "heavy" or "painful" as David's response to being completely known. This simply blanks the psalm's unseen wording, leaving the baker to guess or already know verse 6.

The setup establishes only that David pictures himself by the farthest sea. It does not establish what God's hand will do there, and God's presence alone does not distinguish "guide" from "warn." The blank therefore tests the unseen wording of verse 10 rather than a meaning the baker can reason out.

The preceding card sets up David's request to be searched and tested, but it does not establish the particular kind of way he asks God to find. "Offensive" is supplied only by the unseen wording of verse 24, making this a wording cloze rather than an inference from the setup.

This poetry question asks the baker to complete the wording of David's line, "stir up ___ all day long." The opening card does not establish the men's all-day warmongering, so the baker cannot reason out "war" rather than "fear" or "doubt" from what has been told.

The blank asks the baker to supply the next words of David's simile, "sharpen their tongues like ___." This is wording completion of the psalm's line rather than a question about what the poisonous-speech picture means.

This question asks for the unseen wording of verse 9, "the trouble their own ___ have caused." The immediately preceding story card sets up only the heads of David's enemies; it does not set up the connection between their speech and the trouble coming back on them.

Both blanks require the baker to guess the wording of verse 11. The preceding card quotes verse 10's burning coals, fire and pits, but gives no basis for reasoning out the new terms "slanderer" and "calamity," including the new picture of calamity hunting someone down.
Nothing in the opening card lets the baker reason that the city is Jerusalem rather than Babylon or Nineveh. This fill-in-the-blank simply asks for the unseen wording of verse 2.
Verse 6 has not yet been told, and the earlier cards give no basis for choosing "forever" over "an age." The baker must guess unseen wording rather than reason out the blank's meaning.

Verse 13 has not yet been told, and the earlier cards do not establish that God's name alone is exalted. There is no reasoned basis for choosing "only" over "oldest" or "royal," so the blank tests unseen wording.

The setup says only that the LORD adorns or dresses up the afflicted. Nothing in the earlier cards lets the baker reason out "salvation"; the baker must guess the unseen wording from three possibilities.

Saying only that the psalm "turns serious" gives no reasoned path from praises in the saints' mouths to a sword in their hands. Choosing sword rather than scroll or torch is therefore a guess at an unseen detail.

Both blanks ask for wording from verse 1 that the baker has not seen, and the earlier card provides no context from which to reason out Solomon and David. The baker must rely on outside recall or guess rather than reason out the meaning.

The earlier cards do not connect hating knowledge with choosing not to fear the LORD. Since praising and thanking the LORD are also things these people could plausibly have neglected, the baker must guess the unseen wording rather than reason out the blank's meaning from the setup.

The preceding cards discuss receiving the father's words and gaining many years of life, but say nothing about what his paths are like. The baker has no contextual basis for choosing straight over winding or hidden; the blank asks for the unseen BSB adjective rather than a meaning the baker can reason out.

Card 3 says that the wicked are out to make someone fall, but it gives no hint about sleep or sleeplessness. The baker cannot reason out sleep rather than work from the earlier cards, so this blank tests the unseen wording of verse 16.

Nothing in the earlier cards lets the baker reason that the wicked man sows discord rather than fear or envy. The blank asks for an unseen word from Proverbs 6:14 instead of testing a meaning the baker can work out.

rule.text: Always give context in the question. The story card before it isn't on screen anymore, so the question says who and what. Never "him," "that" or "it" pointing back to a card the baker can't see.

examples: The phrase "that tree" points back to choice card 15, which the baker can no longer see. Make the question self-contained by identifying the forbidden tree.
“All of that” points back to the three descriptions on story card 9, which is no longer on screen. The question needs to supply the relevant context itself.
“After this” depends on the preceding story card, which is no longer visible. The question does not identify the statement or event that “this” refers to, so it is not self-contained.

places.problem: The phrase "that tree" points back to choice card 15, which the baker can no longer see. Make the question self-contained by identifying the forbidden tree.
“All of that” points back to the three descriptions on story card 9, which is no longer on screen. The question needs to supply the relevant context itself.
“After this” depends on the preceding story card, which is no longer visible. The question does not identify the statement or event that “this” refers to, so it is not self-contained.
“That altar” depends on the previous card for its antecedent. Standing alone, the question does not identify the altar at the site between Bethel and Ai.
“That plain” points back to earlier cards instead of identifying the plain within the question itself. The question should supply the context, such as naming the plain of the Jordan.

The phrase "answer for this" points back to Sarai's accusation on the previous story card without saying what Abram is responding to. The question needs to summarize that complaint so it stands on its own.
"That promise" points back to card 13, which is no longer on screen. The question should restate that Jacob has promised that anyone found with Laban's gods will not live.
The question relies on the preceding story card to identify "her" as Potiphar's wife and to explain what Joseph is refusing. The question itself does not provide that context.
"Says it again" points back to an earlier card for what Potiphar's wife says. The question should restate that she again demands that Joseph sleep with her.
"In her story" never identifies Potiphar's wife, leaving the question dependent on earlier cards for its context.

The question begins with “After them,” but the antecedent is available only on the preceding story card. It also does not identify the moment as Pharaoh’s dream, so the question is not self-contained.
The phrase “what to do about it” points back to earlier cards without identifying what Pharaoh must act on. The question needs to supply the context of the coming abundance and famine itself.
"All that forced labor" points back to the preceding card instead of identifying the Israelites' forced labor in Egypt, so the question relies on context the baker can no longer see.

"This time" and "the same thing" do not identify the Nile being turned to blood. The question depends on context from cards that are no longer on screen instead of saying what the magicians are supposedly unable to repeat.
The question depends on "that son" and an unspecified "they" from the preceding card. It does not independently identify the Israelite son who asks what the firstborn practice means.
The question uses "it" without identifying what Moses is to write down. That depends on earlier cards, so the question does not stand alone; it should identify the battle or victory being recorded.
"Write it on a scroll" again leaves the pronoun's antecedent on an earlier card. The question should say what Moses is recording rather than relying on context the baker cannot see.

Choice cards 3, 5, 6 and 9 refer to the Israelites only as 'them' or 'they,' without identifying the group within the question. Since the preceding story card is no longer on screen, each question needs to identify who God is addressing.
"That land" points back to the preceding story card. The question does not identify it as the land God's angel is bringing Israel into, so the question is not self-contained.
"They" has no antecedent within the question. The question itself needs to identify the Israelites as the people serving God.
"Them" has no antecedent within the question. It should name the Israelites rather than relying on the preceding cards to identify who will have sickness taken away.
The question is not self-contained. “That velvet rope” points back to the previous story card, and the question does not identify Moses or the invited leaders whose access is being limited.
The question relies on the preceding story card with "that veil" instead of identifying the tabernacle veil within the question itself.
The question points back to card 12 with "that oil" and does not identify the pure olive oil for the tabernacle light within the question itself.

The question does not stand on its own. "Right after that" and "this" point back to the preceding story card without identifying God's instructions about the undergarments and ministering at the Tent of Meeting or altar.

"In that message" points back to the message introduced on story card 8, which is no longer on screen. The question should identify the LORD's message to the Israelites without relying on that earlier card.
"That rock" points back to the rock introduced on story card 16. The question should supply its own context, such as identifying it as the rock near the LORD where Moses is standing.
The question never identifies who 'they' and 'them' are. Eleazar and Ithamar were named on the previous card, which is no longer visible, so the question does not provide its own context.
The question does not identify whose purification it describes. Its 'her' and 'she' depend on earlier cards, rather than naming the woman and giving the childbirth context within the question itself.

The wording 'After a daughter, she...' leaves 'she' without an on-card antecedent and does not clearly state that this is the woman who has given birth to a daughter. The question relies on context that is no longer on screen.

The question is not self-contained. "When it's a maybe" uses "it" and "maybe" to point back to the white-spot scenario on story card 4, which is no longer on screen. The choice card itself never explains what condition is being isolated.

Choice cards 10, 11 and 13 depend on "This day" or "this day" without identifying which day they mean. The date was introduced back on story card 8, which is no longer on screen. Each question should carry enough context itself, such as identifying the day of atonement or the tenth day of the seventh month.
The question is not self-contained: "those trees" points back to the previous story card without identifying them as the fruit trees Israel will plant when they enter the land.
The question depends on unseen earlier cards: "this plan" does not explain the fruit-tree timeline, and "their harvest" does not identify Israel.
The phrase "like that" points back to the previous choice card instead of stating within this question how Israel is to treat and love the foreigner.
The question depends on “that priest” in the previous card. It does not explain that this is a priest who became unclean by touching something defiling, so the statement is not self-contained.
“At the end of that warning” points back to card 11 without telling the baker what the warning was. The question needs to supply the context of God warning the priests to keep His charge.

“That daughter” depends on card 16. The question never identifies her as a priest's daughter who married a man other than a priest, which is necessary context for the statement about sharing her father's food.
“That young animal” and “the eighth day” depend on card 12. The question does not identify a newborn ox, sheep, or goat or explain that the eighth day is counted from its birth.

Choice cards 2, 5 and 6 rely on "that struggling countryman" or "That countryman" pointing back to earlier cards. The questions do not independently identify the destitute Israelite who sold himself, even though the earlier story cards are no longer visible.
"With harvests like that" depends on the preceding story card to explain what "like that" means. Once that card is no longer on screen, the question is not self-contained.
"That day in Egypt" depends on the preceding story card for its meaning. Standing alone, the question never identifies which day or event in Egypt it means.
"On that day" again leaves the question without its own context. It should identify the day as the one when the LORD struck down Egypt's firstborn rather than pointing back to an unseen card.
The question is not self-contained: "this command" points back to earlier cards without identifying the command to send the three groups outside the camp.
"That person" points back to the preceding card rather than identifying the person in the question itself. It should establish that this is someone guilty of sinning against another person.

The question begins "While she holds the grain offering" without identifying who "she" is. The antecedent appears only on the preceding story card, which is no longer visible; the question should identify her as the woman or wife.

The question says "If no other man has slept with her" without identifying the woman. It relies on the preceding story card for the antecedent instead of supplying that context in the question itself.

"Under that oath" points back to the oath introduced on the preceding story card, which the baker can no longer see. The question should name the oath of the curse and identify the woman rather than relying on "that oath" and the unidentified "her."
The phrase "that line" depends on the preceding card. On its own, the question does not identify the boundary as coming near the furnishings of the sanctuary or the altar.

The phrase "this portion" points back to the preceding story card without identifying what the portion is. The question should supply the context, such as the portion of the Israelites' sacred offerings.
The question relies on "that first count," whose meaning comes from earlier cards that are no longer visible. It should identify the Sinai count within the question itself.

The question never identifies what "this move" or "it" means. The needed action, discouraging Israel from crossing into the land, appears only on earlier cards. Restate that action so the question stands on its own.

"Do all that" sends the baker back to the conditions on story card 1, which is no longer visible. The question should restate that the Gadites and Reubenites must arm themselves and cross the Jordan for battle.
The question relies on the preceding, now-hidden cards to identify "those people." The question itself needs to identify them as the inhabitants of Canaan whom Israel might allow to remain.

The phrase "a deadly weapon like that" points back to the preceding story card, which is no longer visible. The question needs to identify the iron object, deadly stone and deadly wooden object itself.

Choice cards 3, 5, 7 and 9 are not self-contained. They refer to Israel only as 'they,' 'them' or 'their,' without an antecedent in the question, so the pronouns depend on earlier cards that are no longer visible. Each question should identify Israel in its own wording.

"That kind of heart" points back to the preceding story card, which is no longer on screen. The question needs to stand on its own by describing the heart God desires: a heart to fear Him and keep His commandments.
"Those images" points back to stop 2 card 17, which is no longer visible. The question needs to identify them as the images of the nations' gods so that its context stands on its own.

The question says the LORD is "also doing it," but the antecedent of "it" is on the preceding card, which is no longer visible. The question needs to identify the action itself, such as driving out the nations or bringing Israel into the land.

The question is not self-contained: "Right after that" points back to the previous, off-screen card, and "them" and "their" never identify Israel. Coming immediately after the list of tithe recipients, the pronouns could also sound like they refer to the Levite, foreigner, fatherless and widow rather than to Israel. The question should name Israel and the third-year tithe explicitly.

The question is not self-contained. "That generous giving" points back to the previous story card, and neither the giver and recipient nor the people represented by "them" are identified in the question.

The question asks about "this command" without identifying which command it means. It depends on the preceding cards to supply the servant-release and provision context instead of stating that context itself.

The words "this is how" point back to the treatment described on story card 6, which is no longer on screen. The question never says what that treatment was, so it does not give enough context on its own.

The question is not self-contained: "that valley" points back to the preceding story card. Identify the setting within the question, such as the valley with running water where the elders bring the heifer.
"Part of this" does not identify what the priests are part of without the preceding story card. The question should name the heifer ceremony at the stream so it stands on its own.

"That declaration" relies on the previous story card without identifying what the elders declared. Give enough of the declaration's setting or content for the true-or-false statement to be understood independently.
The question does not establish who "his" and "he" refer to. It should identify the man who brought the captive woman into his house and wants to marry her rather than relying on the earlier cards.

Several questions depend on context that is no longer on screen. Stop 1 card 9 says "the other's clothing" without identifying the woman and man; stop 2 card 8 refers to "the accusation" without explaining it; stop 2 card 12 says "both of them" without identifying the man and betrothed woman or their encounter; and stop 2 card 15 refers to "the open-country case" without restating what happened.
The question refers to "the widow" without explaining the family situation. It depends on the previous story card to establish that a brother died without a son and another brother married his widow.
"If the brother refuses" does not say what he refuses to do or identify his relationship to the widow. The question only makes full sense with the preceding story card.

"His family name" has no antecedent within the question. The baker must rely on earlier cards to know that this is the brother who refused to marry his brother's widow and went through the sandal ceremony.
The question depends on "that altar" to identify which altar Moses is discussing. Since the preceding story card is no longer on screen, the question should identify it as the altar on Mount Ebal.
The question depends on 'that faraway nation' and an unidentified 'they' from the preceding card. Standing alone, it should identify Israel and the nation neither Israel nor its fathers have known.

'That nation' points back to an earlier card instead of identifying the nation within the question. The question should supply the needed context, such as the ruthless nation from far away that is attacking Israel.

'Sink that low' points back to the cannibalism on the preceding story card without saying what the behavior is. The question is not self-contained; it needs to describe the desperate eating and refusal to share during the siege.

The question asks what "they" promise without identifying the speakers. The Reubenites, the Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh are named only on earlier cards, so the question does not supply its own context.
"Then they tell Joshua" leaves the speakers unidentified and depends on earlier cards for the antecedent of "they." The question should identify the tribes speaking to Joshua.
"Then they get serious" does not identify who is speaking. The question relies on earlier cards to establish that "they" are the Reubenites, the Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh.
"On that evening" points back to card 13 for the date, but that story card is no longer visible. The question should identify the evening within its own wording.
"These things" has no antecedent within the question and points back to the previous card, so the question does not supply its own context.
"After this" points back to the preceding story card without identifying the event, leaving the question dependent on context the baker can no longer see.
"Behind them" and "their city" have no antecedent in the question; they rely on the preceding story card to identify the men of Ai. Name the men of Ai in the question itself.
"According to that book" points back to card 17 instead of identifying the Book of Jashar in the question itself.
The opening words "The elders say that's exactly why they came" use "that" to point back to Jephthah's question on card 10, which is no longer on screen. The question needs to restate that context.
"That land" points back to the description on story card 3, which is no longer on screen. The question itself does not identify the land or restate the king's claim that Israel seized it.

The question is not self-contained. In "Once they know it was Samson," the word "it" depends on the preceding story card for what Samson did; the question itself never mentions his burning the Philistines' crops.
"That place" has no antecedent within the question. Identifying the place where Samson fought requires earlier cards that are no longer on screen.

The question never identifies who "They" are. The preceding story card refers only to "the party" and "their hearts," so the question itself does not establish that the Philistines are bringing Samson out.
The question relies on "that spot," pointing back to the directions on story card 4, which is no longer on screen. Repeat the identifying context in the question so it stands on its own.

The question depends on "those men" without identifying them. Their identity appears only on the previous card, which the baker can no longer see; this question should identify them as the men who said Saul should not reign.

"If Saul hears that" points back to the Bethlehem excuse on the preceding story card. The question needs to summarize that excuse itself so it remains self-contained when the story card is no longer visible.

"That second day" relies on the preceding story card for its meaning. The question should identify the second day of the New Moon meal or month so the baker has the necessary context on the choice card itself.
The question begins, "By the time they've all gathered," but never identifies who "they" are. That antecedent is available only on the preceding story card, which is no longer on screen.
The word "them" points back to David's father and mother on the previous card rather than identifying them within this question. The question should supply its own context.

The question does not stand on its own once the preceding story card disappears. "This stranger" does not identify Saul, and "his request" does not say that he asked the medium to consult a spirit and bring someone up.
The question depends on card 14 for essential context. "Those men" and "this" do not identify the men or their plan to withhold plunder from the two hundred who stayed behind.
"The woman" has no antecedent on the choice card. Without the previous story card, the question does not identify her as the woman David saw bathing from the palace roof.
"If the king asks all that" points back to Joab's expected questions on earlier cards instead of giving the necessary context on this card.
The phrase "on that rock" points back to the preceding story card, which is no longer on screen. The question needs to supply the rock and vigil context itself rather than relying on that reference.
The phrase "If Solomon walks that way" points back to earlier cards without explaining how Solomon is to walk. The question does not stand on its own.
The question never identifies Solomon or his sons as the ones who might turn away. It depends on the preceding story card to supply who is being warned.
The words "they" and "their" have no antecedent in the question. The baker must rely on earlier cards to know that Israel forsook the LORD and that the fathers were Israel's fathers.

Shown on its own, this question does not identify what the queen saw or what the report concerned. "She's seen it" and "the report" send the baker back to earlier cards for the basic context instead of naming Solomon and his wisdom and prosperity.
"This turn of events" points back to the preceding story card instead of identifying Rehoboam's refusal to listen to the people. The question does not supply its own context.
The question relies on earlier cards to identify "the warriors" as Rehoboam's forces and to explain what "this" refers to. Neither the who nor the what is established within the question itself.

The question is not self-contained: “that demand” points back to card 3, which is no longer visible, without restating that Ben-hadad has demanded Ahab's wealth and family. Put the demand in the question rather than referring back to the earlier card.
"That man" points back to the archer introduced only on card 9, so the question does not stand on its own when that story card is off screen.
"After that" points back to the feast and send-off on card 17 without identifying them in the question. The question should name the event it refers to so it stands alone.
The question depends on 'that story,' pointing back to card 11 instead of identifying Gehazi's account of Elisha bringing the dead back to life. The earlier card is no longer on screen.

The phrases 'about it' and 'the story' never identify what the king asks the woman to confirm. The question needs to supply the context that Gehazi has identified her and the son Elisha restored to life.

The question depends on "Hazael hears this" and "such a monstrous thing," but it never says what Elisha has just told him. These phrases point back to card 12, so the question does not supply its own context once that story card is off screen.
The phrase "that plot of ground" has no antecedent within the question and depends on the preceding cards, which are no longer on screen. The question needs to identify Naboth's plot itself.

The question begins with “They” without identifying the people of the land. The pronoun's antecedent is only on the preceding story card, which is no longer on screen, so the question does not supply its own context.
The question is not self-contained. "Them" refers to the people around the king, who are identified only on the preceding story card, which is no longer on screen.
The question's "they" has no antecedent within the question. Identifying who acts depends on earlier cards that are no longer visible.
"After that" points back to the preceding story card about Zedekiah's eyes being put out, so the question does not supply that context itself.
"Them all" has no antecedent in the question. The baker must rely on the preceding story card to know that Nebuzaradan is bringing the priests and other officials.

Several questions do not carry their own context. Card 12 relies on "the three tribes," card 14 on "that battle," card 18 on "these families," and card 20 on "these tribes," rather than identifying the people or event within the question.
The question does not identify who "them" refers to. Its antecedent is on the preceding story card, which is no longer visible, so the question lacks the context needed to stand on its own.
The question depends on the preceding story card to identify "The crown." Once that card is gone, the question does not say that this is the crown David took from the Ammonite king.
The question does not identify David or Solomon. "This son" depends on earlier cards that are no longer visible, so the question does not supply its own context.
The wording "While they praise the LORD" leaves "they" without an antecedent within the choice card. It points back to the trumpeters and singers on earlier cards that the baker can no longer see.

The question leaves "them" unidentified and omits the shut skies and lack of rain. Without the previous story card on screen, the question does not establish who Solomon is asking God to forgive or the drought context that makes "rain" a reasoned answer.

"That enemy land" and "they" point back to the previous story card. The question never identifies the captive Israelites who have come to their senses and returned to God, so it is not self-contained.

Several questions rely on antecedents from cards that are no longer visible. Card 5 says "hard days like that," card 7 says "do all that," card 16 says "If it comes to that," and card 17 says "did this" without identifying the disaster in the question.

The question begins with "They," but never identifies who they are. With the preceding story card no longer on screen, the baker cannot tell from the question whether this means the priests and Levites, the people from every tribe, or all the newcomers together.
The question uses "they" without identifying who returns to Jerusalem, so it depends on the previous story card for its subject. It should name Jehoshaphat and the men of Judah and Jerusalem.
The phrase "Along with that help" points back to the preceding card instead of making the question self-contained. The question should restate the assistance Cyrus has just described.
"They" has no antecedent within the question. The question relies on card 1 to identify the returning exiles instead of supplying that context itself.
"When they arrive" has no antecedent within the question. It should identify the returned exiles rather than depending on earlier cards to establish who "they" are.
